title: Shoes, tables and the rest of the kit
seo_title: Table tennis shoes, tables and clothing: what you need
description: What to wear and what to play on: table tennis shoes and clothing, the official table and net sizes, and how to choose an indoor or outdoor table for home.
summary: Beyond a bat and balls you need indoor shoes with good grip and comfortable sportswear. If you want a table at home, here is what the rules say and what to look for.
key_points: Wear indoor shoes with a grippy, non-marking sole; specialist table tennis shoes are built for quick sideways and forward-and-back movement.
Match clothing is a short-sleeved or sleeveless shirt with shorts or a skirt, in a colour clearly different from the ball.
A regulation table is 2.74m long, 1.525m wide and 76cm high, with a net 15.25cm high.
Competition tables have 25mm tops; outdoor tables use weatherproof tops such as aluminium composite.
A ball dropped from 30cm should bounce about 23cm on a good table, a test you can do in the shop.
body: To play table tennis you need little beyond a bat and balls: indoor shoes with a grippy sole, and light sportswear in a colour that contrasts with the ball. A table of your own is optional, since clubs and leisure centres provide them. If you do buy one, a regulation table is 2.74m long, 1.525m wide and 76cm high, and the thickness of the top decides how well it plays.
## Shoes

Table tennis is a game of short, sharp movements: forward to a short ball, back for a loop, sideways to cover the wide angles. Butterfly, which makes shoes for the sport, says its models are designed for indoor competition and have high grip on the outer sole because the game involves so much intense front-to-back and side-to-side movement. Mizuno, another maker, sells its Wave Medal range as lightweight indoor shoes with cushioning and stability.

You don't need specialist shoes to start. Any clean indoor trainers with non-marking soles and a good grip will do. Look for a shoe that holds your foot firmly when you push off sideways, and keep it for indoors only. Buy table tennis shoes once you play every week.
## Clothing

For a club night, wear whatever you would wear for a gym session. For matches, the ITTF regulations set out a simple dress code: a short-sleeved or sleeveless shirt and shorts or a skirt, or a one-piece sports outfit, with socks and playing shoes. Anything else, such as a tracksuit, needs the referee's permission.

The main colour of your shirt and shorts or skirt must be clearly different from the colour of the ball in use, which is white or orange. Opponents must wear shirts different enough to tell apart; if both players turn up in similar shirts and cannot agree who changes, the umpire decides by lot. Clothing must not carry bright reflective markings that could unsight an opponent, or anything offensive. Check your league's rules, but a plain coloured playing shirt is a safe choice.
## The official table

Law 2.1 of the ITTF's laws defines the table. The playing surface is 2.74m long and 1.525m wide, in a horizontal plane 76cm above the floor. It can be made of any material, but it must give a uniform bounce of about 23cm when a standard ball is dropped on to it from 30cm. The surface must be dark and matt, with a 2cm white line along each edge, and doubles adds a 3mm white centre line down the middle.

The net is 15.25cm high along its whole length, and its posts stand 15.25cm outside the side lines, so it overhangs the table. A net that sags in the middle or sits lower at one end changes the game, so check it before you play. Our guide to [the rules](/guide/table-tennis-rules-explained.html) explains what happens when a ball clips the net or the edge.
## Choosing a table for home

The most important figure is the thickness of the top. Competition tables used in clubs and tournaments have 25mm tops. Donic's Waldner Classic 25, for example, has a 25mm top and is ITTF approved and built to the European standard EN 14468-1, class A, for high-performance sport. Tables like that weigh more than 100kg and cost from several hundred pounds to more than £1,000.

If a table's top is thinner than 25mm, or the maker doesn't say how thick it is, the bounce is the test that matters. Drop a ball from 30cm, about the height of a ruler, at different points on the table: on a good one it should come back to roughly 23cm everywhere, with no dead spots near the edges or the legs.

Look for a table that folds and rolls on wheels with brakes, so you can store it easily. Measure your room first, allowing space behind each end as well as for the table itself. The ITTF minimum playing space for international events is 14m long, 7m wide and 5m high, which few homes can match.
## Outdoor tables

Indoor tables are not made to be left out in the rain. Outdoor tables use weatherproof tops and rust-resistant frames: Stiga's XTR outdoor table, for example, has a 6mm aluminium composite top, galvanised steel and exterior-grade powder coating. Do the bounce test on an outdoor table too, and buy a cover: Stiga recommends one to extend a table's life.
## The rest of the kit

A few small things make a difference. A bat case protects your rubbers when the bat is in your bag. A small towel lets you dry your hands and face during breaks. A box of your own balls is useful for practice, and our [guide to balls](/guide/table-tennis-balls-explained.html) explains which to buy. Bring a water bottle.

Lighting matters too, if you set up at home. For major events the ITTF says light should be at least 1,800 lux vertically and 2,000 lux horizontally, with the light source at least 5m above the floor and a generally dark background with no daylight from uncovered windows, so the ball stands out. You will not match that in a garage, but bright, even light and covered windows help.
## Your next steps

If you have not chosen a bat yet, start with [what bat a beginner should buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html). Then take your new shoes to a club: our guide to [finding a club in England](/guide/find-a-table-tennis-club-england.html) explains how.
